From the Chairman…

Annual Report 2022–23

The year 2023 marks a watershed for India as it celebrates 75 years of independence and ushers its people into the 
Amrit Kaal of transforming into a developed nation by 2047. At this critical juncture of history in the making, India’s 
development vision and economic heft take the global centre stage as it assumes the Presidency of G20, imbued with 
spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (One Earth, One Family, One Future), upholding green development, inclusive 
and resilient growth as its priorities.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 7]
Family, One Future), upholding green development, inclusive 
and resilient growth as its priorities.

In a year marked by tremendous geopolitical turmoil and supply shocks leading to slowdown in growth, high 
and persistent inflation, and many uncertainties clouding the global economic outlook, India has shown remarkable 
resilience. It has turned the challenge into an opportunity by preparing a blueprint to steer the economy towards a 
golden era. In this milieu, NABARD entered its fifth decade as a development finance institution dedicated to serving 
India’s key developmental goals and spurring rural prosperity.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 7]
nce institution dedicated to serving 
India’s key developmental goals and spurring rural prosperity.

Our utmost priority lies in addressing the inter-regional disparity in agriculture credit particularly in terms of the 
east, north-east, and central regions (having a credit share of only 24% despite a gross cropped area share of 44%). 
In order to address inequity in access to credit, especially by women and small and marginal farmers, NABARD has 
been spearheading their collectivisation and inclusion into the formal banking system. The flagship Self Help Group–
Bank Linkage Programme (SHG–BLP) and credit linkage of joint liability groups (JLGs) have been instrumental in 
delivering credit to the last mile. We are proud to have empowered rural women from 16.2 crore households so far by 
assisting them to save, borrow and foray into enterprise. NABARD is also actively innovating and striving to realise 
the full potential of SHGs and graduate them into farmer producers’ organisations (FPOs) and micro-enterprises to 
generate sustainable livelihood alternatives that enable economic and

Over the years, NABARD has diligently expanded and shaped the ecosystem for formal credit, 
microfinance, and cooperation in rural India with support from governments, the Reserve Bank of India 
(RBI), partner agencies and other stakeholders. To strengthen rural financial institutions (particularly 
cooperatives) and make them impactful, it is imperative to embrace digitalisation. Digitalisation can 
help secure higher agricultural earnings by reducing information asymmetry across farmers, suppliers, 
retailers, consumers, bankers, and other stakeholders in a cost-effective manner. In this direction, 
NABARD, in collaboration with the Government of India (GOI), is implementing the centrally sponsored 
scheme for the computerisation of 63,000 primary agricultural credit societies over the next 5 years to 
facilitate the adoption of core banking solutions by cooperatives, faster transactions, unhindered access 
to payment services and more effective supervision. Furthermore, this year NA

set up its own enterprise data warehouse to store data generated within the organisation and derive 
detailed analytics-based insights to cater to the diverse needs of rural India.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 8]
nisation and derive 
detailed analytics-based insights to cater to the diverse needs of rural India.

Post-harvest losses and volatility in the prices of agricultural commodities—especially perishables 
like tomato, onion and potato—due to lack of storage infrastructure have been distressful for farmers 
and consumers alike. The government of India’s plan to build the world’s largest networked foodgrain 
storage structures in the cooperative sector will help in checking distress sales by farmers, reduce import 
dependence and create employment opportunities in rural India. We, at NABARD, have stepped up 
efforts to make this mammoth exercise a success. We have initiated a pilot project in 11 states entailing 
the setting up of grain storage infrastructure along with other agri-infrastructure. This will act as a 
catalyst for enhancing farmers’ income given the possible synergies between this programme, the central 
sector scheme to promote 10,000 FPOs and electronic-Negotiable Warehouse Receipts.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 8]
mme, the central 
sector scheme to promote 10,000 FPOs and electronic-Negotiable Warehouse Receipts.

True to its mandate, NABARD has been a pioneer of impact investments and innovations in areas 
of financing rural infrastructure. Over the years, rural infrastructure funding to state governments has 
reached a cumulative sanction of ₹5 lakh crore for 7.7 lakh projects in agriculture, rural connectivity, and 
social sector. Our flagship Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) has had a transformational 
impact on the rural landscape by creating irrigation potential of 376 lakh hectare, laying 5.4 lakh 
kilometre of rural roads, building 13.3 lakh metre of rural bridges, and generating 3,029.2 crore person 
days of non-recurring employment.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 8]
 lakh metre of rural bridges, and generating 3,029.2 crore person 
days of non-recurring employment.

With a special focus on reducing regional socioeconomic imbalances, NABARD is also promoting 
capital formation by leveraging public and private investment through various funds viz., RIDF, NABARD 
Infrastructure Development Assistance, Credit Facility for Federations, Direct Refinance Assistance, Dairy 
Processing & Infrastructure Development Fund, Fisheries and Aquaculture Infrastructure Development 
Fund, Warehouse Infrastructure Fund, etc. For achieving greater efficiency and transparency in the 
usage of funds, NABARD has launched the digital application of NABPARIKSHAN during the year to 
actively monitor and verify the assets, which have been refinanced by NABARD.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 8]
AN during the year to 
actively monitor and verify the assets, which have been refinanced by NABARD.

Climate change, as a major global risk, has emerged as the most potent challenge for the sustainable 
development of Indian agriculture. Therefore, adaptation to and mitigation of climate change impact 
through better management of natural resources, crop diversification, integrated nutrient management, 
etc. are central to making agriculture sustainable. Towards this end, we have taken initiatives towards 
accomplishing social, economic, and environmental sustainability and playing our role in supporting our 
country in achieving the United Nations’ mandated Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. NABARD 
has promoted watershed and tribal development programmes through grant support, which encouraged 
soil and water conservation and the development of agroforestry. Further, NABARD in the capacity of 
National Implementing Entity and Direct Access Entity for three important climate funds has played 
a significant role in promoting climate-resilient agricultural practices by funding of 4

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 8]
has played

a significant role in promoting climate-resilient agricultural practices by funding of 40 such projects 
involving ₹1,852.6 crore.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 9]
From the Chairman …
vii

Realising the importance of climate resilient agriculture, the United Nations has declared 2023 as 
the ‘International Year of Millets’. With favourable agronomic and socio-cultural conditions, millets 
present a unique opportunity for India to move beyond food security towards nutritional security. 
NABARD has also intensified engagement with millet cultivators through the capacity building of 
FPOs and convergence and collaborations with other stakeholders. Given the nutritional benefits and 
market potential of millets, NABARD has dedicated a theme chapter on millets in this Annual Report for 
spreading awareness and ensuring effective plan implementation.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 9]
n millets in this Annual Report for 
spreading awareness and ensuring effective plan implementation.

Since its inception, NABARD has facilitated inclusive and sustainable rural growth by supplementing 
and complementing the initiatives of the government and other stakeholders. We have deployed 
innovative models to strengthen the ecosystem for credit in the rural hinterland and develop grassroots 
institutions (SHGs, JLGs, and FPOs), supporting social sectors through refinance and concessional 
credit and developing sustainable models for promoting livelihood.

NABARD has ended the 2023 fiscal on a strong and introspective note, drawing out its first strategic 
plan document christened ‘Pragati 1.0, Beyond Tomorrow: NABARD@2028,’ a well-thought-out 
institutional response on how we plan to forge ahead over in next 5 years.

[Annual Report 2022-23 | PDF page 9]
028,’ a well-thought-out 
institutional response on how we plan to forge ahead over in next 5 years.

NABARD sincerely acknowledges the cooperation extended by GOI, RBI, our banking partners, rural 
financial institutions, cooperatives, civil society organisations, other development partners, and, above 
all, the farming communities and rural populations of India. On behalf of NABARD, I express hope and 
confidence that we will continue our constructive role in formulating effective policy frameworks and 
piloting interventions with ever-greater energy.

It is my belief that this journey of NABARD in supporting rural India’s overall economic development; 
building a more resilient agriculture and rural sector; and positively impacting the lives of farmers and 
rural populations will deepen, widen, and become more meaningful in the years to come.

Shaji K. V.

Chairman

The year in context

The year witnessed global economic turmoil caused by multiple, complex, and interconnected 
crises. A series of severe and mutually reinforcing shocks in the last 3 years, such as the COVID-19 
pandemic, food and energy crises precipitated by the war in Ukraine, surging inflation, debt 
tightening, and climate emergency, coalesced into what experts have called a ‘polycrisis’ that

battered the world economy in FY2023.

India showed resilience in countering the pandemic and staging a recovery in FY2022 ahead of 
many other major economies. In FY2023, while it positioned itself to supersede the pre-pandemic 
growth path, it was also faced with the challenge of reining in inflation caused by geopolitical 
events and interconnected shocks.

1.1.1	 Global economic outlook

In the run-up to FY2023, pandemic and the Russia–
Ukraine war disrupted the global supply chain; food, 
fuel, and fertiliser prices rose sharply; and inflationary 
pressures mounted. As a result, most of the major 
economies scrambled for synchronised monetary policy 
tightening with severe consequences for economic growth 
globally. Global inflation, which was 8.7% in FY2022,

globally. Global inflation, which was 8.7% in FY2022,

decreased to 7% in FY2023 and is expected to dip to 4.9% 
in FY2024.1 Decrease in overall inflation is mainly due 
to the tightening of monetary policy by the central banks 
in many emerging and developed economies. Monetary 
tightening has a trade-off with economic growth, hence 
in FY2023, global growth slowed to 2.8% from 3.4% in 
FY2022; however, it is expected to rise to 3% in FY2024.2 
Europe and the United States are suffering more from the 
slow down as compared to Asian economies which have 
better prospects given greater investments and lower

1.1.2	 Domestic economic outlook

High frequency indicators such as the global 
purchasing managers index (PMI) for manufacturing 
have been showing positive signs in the last few months. 
The PMI has made remarkable recovery from the dip in 
sentiment during the pandemic to attain pre-pandemic 
levels and surpass it post February 2023.10 Similarly, 
the index of industrial production (IIP) stood at 151.4 
in March 2023, the highest in the last 2 years. The 
IIP for mining stood at 154.2 in March 2023, while 
manufacturing was at 147.1 and electricity at 188. The 
IIP for March 2023 and PMI trends both indicate a 
healthy outlook for the manufacturing sector.11

Inflationary concerns

The Indian economy regained its position as the fastest 
growing large economy in the world with the strong 
recovery in FY2022 and continued growth momentum 
in FY2023. India’s GDP has grown at a rate of 7.2% (in 
real terms) in FY2023, which is less than the growth rate 
in FY2022 (9.1%),3 mainly due to the base effect (Figure 
1.1). A favourable policy environment and greater focus 
on capital expenditure has resulted in healthy growth of 
11.4% in investment to GDP ratio and its share in GDP 
has reached 34% at constant prices.4 Greater investment 
in infrastructure, technology, manufacturing, and 
agriculture sectors could generate the momentum 
needed for faster and more sustainable growth in the 
long run. The increase in capital expenditure by 37.4% 
over FY2022 (envisioned in the Union Budget for 
FY2024) will further boost investment and long-term 
growth of the economy.

India has never been in the league of export-led economies 
such as South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore. 
However, contrary to perception, India is also seen to

and this aggregate performance has co-existed with 
underperformance in unskilled manufacturing exports, 
which has resulted in at least $140 billion in ‘missing’ 
unskilled economic activity annually.24 During the last few 
years, India has been focusing on initiatives to promote 
exports, resulting in strong exports performance despite 
a period of global slowdown and uncertainty.

India needs to spend about $1.4 trillion on infrastructure 
to achieve the medium-term goal of becoming a 
$5 trillion economy.28 The GOI launched the National 
Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) in FY2020 with a projected 
infrastructure investment of around $1.5 trillion 
(₹111 lakh crore) during 2020–2025 to provide world-
class infrastructure across the country and to improve 
the quality of life for all citizens. Global experience 
has shown that a dollar spent by the government for 
infrastructure investment raises domestic welfare by 
equivalent of $0.8 of private consumption.29 The NIP was 
launched with 6,835 projects, which has now expanded 
to over 9,000 projects covering 34 infrastructure sub-
sectors. During 2020–2025, sectors such as energy 
(24%), roads (19%), urban (16%), and railways (13%) 
would account for around 70% of the projected capital

Millets are among the oldest foods known to humanity, estimated to have been under cultivation since 8000 
BCE. Millets have traditionally been the main source of income, dietary energy (as the staple), and protein 
for people in arid and semi-arid tropics in the world. Major millets include sorghum (jowar), pearl millet 
(bajra), and finger millet (ragi/mandua) while minor millets include foxtail millet (kangani/kakun), proso 
millet (cheena), kodo millet (kodo), barnyard millet (sawa/sanwa/jhangora), little millet (kutki), and two 
pseudo millets—buckwheat (kuttu) and amaranthus (chaulai).

Though millets have been grown in India for centuries for their nutritional richness, low water and input 
requirement, and climate resilience, area under millet cultivation has decreased significantly since the 
1980s, making space for wheat and rice as the cultivator responded to market demand.

Recognising the hardiness, health benefits, nutritional density, and the suitability of millets to the Indian 
palate and plate, the Government of India has been promoting millet cultivation in recent years. In April 
2018, India rebranded nutrient-rich millets as ‘nutricereals’ and declared the year 2018 as the National 
Year of Millets. India also sponsored the proposal for declaring 2023 as International Year of Millets (IYM), 
which the United Nations General Assembly accepted. Since then, India has been at the forefront of building 
a ‘people’s movement’ around IYM 2023 while positioning itself as the global hub for millets. The Union 
Budget for FY2024 referred to millets as ‘Shree Anna’ or super food (literally, the ‘finest foodgrain’).

2.1	 Trends in area, production, and yield

Despite the enormous benefits of millets, there has been a 
slow but steady shift in the dietary preferences of Indians 
towards rice and wheat in the past 6 decades. Millets 
have been marginalised post the Green Revolution which 
pushed for large-scale rice and wheat cultivation using 
high yielding variety seeds. As a result, millets, which 
made up 20% of Indian food basket up to 1965–1970, 
stand currently at 6%, with a 33.9% decline in area under 
millet cultivation between AY1951 and AY2022.1

The consistent improvement in yield estimates 
over the years indicates the adoption of better farming 
practices in India in the past few decades. Decadal 
percent change in area and production suggests that fall 
in area of millet cultivation was compensated by higher 
yield to maintain higher production (Figure 2.2).

India is the largest millet producer in the world, with 
a share of 44%, followed by China (~9%) and Niger 
(~7%).2 In India, millets are primarily a kharif crop 
mostly grown in rainfed conditions, demanding less 
water and agricultural inputs than other staple crops. 
While the area under millet production has decreased 
to one-third between AY1951 and AY2022, production 
has increased marginally [at the compound annual 
growth rate (CAGR) 0.2%] driven by improvements in 
yield (CAGR 1.7%) with the adoption of better farming 
practices (Figure 2.1).

2.4.3	Improving India’s millet export prospects

In the last 2 years, world export of millets has 
increased from $400 million in 2020 to $470 million in 
2021 (ITC trade map), which led to increase in India’s 
millet export from $63 million (₹469.4 crore) in FY2022 
to $75 million (₹608.1 crore) in FY2023.13

Clientele for Indian millets is concentrated in a 
limited number of countries with the major five export 
destinations being United Arab Emirates (17.8%), Saudi 
Arab (13.7%), Nepal (7.4%), Bangladesh (4.9%), and 
Japan (4.4%). In FY2023, Nepal (89%) was the top 
destination for ragi exports, Egypt (66.3%) for jowar, 
and the United Arab Emirates (54%) for bajra.14

2.5.1	 Millets for marginalised dryland farmers

A study on water productivity mapping of major Indian 
crops indicates that rice, wheat, and sugarcane consume 
80% of the freshwater available in India, leading to 
highly ‘inefficient, iniquitous, and unsustainable use 
of water resources.’16 Millets, on the contrary, are 
hardy, low-cost, and climate- and drought-resilient 
crops. Therefore, millet farming, besides conserving 
biodiversity and water use, also supports the most 
vulnerable of food growers such as women, tribal, small, 
and marginal farmers. Most promotion and branding 
exercises around millet cultivation specifically target 
these growers. Incentivising millet cultivation among 
women and tribal farmers could help achieve not just 
national goals of millet output but also global goals 
related to sustainable agriculture, production, and 
consumption.

Humanity today faces multiple challenges due to climate change crisis, poverty, inequality, and 
biodiversity depletion. The path to sustainable development necessitates a holistic approach that 
will balance the needs of present and future generations and mainstream social, economic, and 
environmental concerns. In this direction, while reducing carbon emissions is the most effective 
and needed climate action, achieving sustainable livelihoods also requires to be focussed on 
simultaneously.

watershed management are good examples of such endeavours that work towards multiple 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). NABARD has also played a pivotal role in funding 
and implementing sustainable climate change adaptation solutions. This chapter charts out 
NABARD’s major initiatives in this sphere.

B.	 Context

‘Ahar-pyne’ is an indigenous irrigation system in South Bihar plains that utilises floodwaters for irrigation purposes. 
An ‘ahar’ is a rectangular water harvesting structure, i.e., a catchment basin embanked on three sides, with the fourth 
side being the natural gradient of the land. ‘Pynes’ are diversion channels drawn from the river for impounding water 
in the ‘ahars’. Water supply for an ahar comes either from natural drainage after rainfall or through pynes. Water for 
irrigation is drawn out by opening outlets made at different heights in the embankment.

C.	 Challenges addressed

Renovation of these 70–80 years old irrigation structures has been supported by the RIDF to improve irrigation 
coverage, recharge groundwater, and increase soil moisture.

D.	 Project components

Embankment protection, step protection, culverts, spillway, head regulator, etc.

On the core premise of achieving rural development through better access to credit, NABARD has, 
over the past 4 decades, catered to the diverse financial needs of communities at the grassroots. 
Our refinance policy and other credit products have led to credit uptick, especially in agriculture, 
and this has been driving growth in foodgrains and horticulture production.

NABARD follows a three-pronged approach to achieving development through credit. First, 
NABARD plays a critical role in the credit planning and monitoring exercise. Second, through its 
refinance and direct finance products, it ensures and enables credit delivery to the last mile. Lastly, 
NABARD is deepening financial inclusion to increase rural credit demand. Our interventions and 
performance along these three prongs during FY2023 comprise the content of this chapter.

6.1	 Credit planning

SFP projection for FY2024, under the priority sector 
across all states is ₹48.2 lakh crore, of which the share 
of agriculture is 47%.

For the agriculture sector (India’s  single largest 
employer) dominated by small and marginal farmers, 
adequate and timely supply of bank credit assumes the 
greatest importance. Therefore, credit planning must 
suitably factor in the demand perspective.

Issues related to infrastructure gaps, credit flow, 
etc., highlighted in the SFP are deliberated upon in 
state credit seminars with participation from state 
government officials, research institutions, and banks. 
Suggestions emanating from these seminars help state 
governments in framing policies and schemes and 
making suitable budgetary provisions.

7.3.1	 Fraud monitoring and review

NABARD has developed an early warning mechanism 
based on an offsite surveillance system (OSS) to alert 
SEs about potential risks. These signals are generated 
by the OSS based on pre-defined financial data and 
ratios and other qualitative indicators captured on a 
continuous basis. A designated nodal officer of NABARD 
ensures the timeliness, completeness, and correctness of 
data submitted by banks in OSS returns. An escalation 
matrix has been designed to initiate supervisory action 
against the bank for inordinate delay/non-submission 
of OSS returns. The final level in the escalation matrix is 
to recommend a penalty on the bank to the RBI.

Empowering Rural 
Financial Institutions

Rural financial institutions (RFIs) comprising rural cooperative banks (RCBs) and regional rural 
banks (RRBs) play a crucial role in financial intermediation in agriculture and rural development.1 
In order to improve the access of banking facilities in rural areas and transform these institutions 
into organisationally strong, financially viable, and operationally efficient entities, NABARD 
endeavours to strengthen the capacity of these institutions through various developmental and 
supervisory initiatives so as to enable them to compete effectively with other financial institutions 
and to purvey ground level credit flow efficiently. It, therefore, closely monitors the RFIs’ business 
growth, profitability, capital adequacy, and non-performing asset (NPA) levels and strengthens 
them through recapitalisation, business diversification, product innovation, digitalisation, etc.

2.7 crore loan accounts. Of the RRB branches, 92% are 
in rural/semi-urban areas.

As on 31 March 2022, RRBs had the highest share of 
current account and savings account deposits (54.5%) 
as a percentage of their total deposits amongst all 
categories of SCBs—public sector banks (43.8%), private 
sector banks (47%), small finance banks (40.5%), and 
foreign banks (43.8%)—putting them at an advantage 
vis-à-vis access to low-cost funds. The fact that almost 
90% of the gross loans outstanding of the RRBs are 
towards priority sectors, speaks of the contribution of 
RRBs to inclusive nation-building (Figure 8.4).

both quantity and quality of any crop between harvest 
and consumption. Assessment of post-harvest losses 
is essential as it depletes food security, nutrition, and 
economic stability. For the Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries, Government of India, during the year, 
NABCONS undertook an assessment of post-harvest 
losses of agri-produce in India.a

sample size of more than 68,000 (farmers/traders/

a company’s management, its board, its shareholders and 
other stakeholders. Corporate governance also provides the 
structure through which the objectives of the company are set,

performance are determined.1 It helps define the way authority 
as well as responsibilities are allocated and how decisions 
are made. Good governance aims at achieving high levels of 
accountability, efficiency, responsibility, transparency, and 
fairness in all areas of operation to increase the confidence of 
investors and other stakeholders.

 | Strengthening of risk management frameworks To enhance risk management frameworks and comply with prudential guidelines on Basel III norms, new polices were framed, revised, and implemented. Automating and streamlining risk management The ERMS project had 22 modules on credit risk and market risk to strengthen the existing risk management framework, assist in identifying a suitable risk management software/system integrator, and provide project management services. The modules are being used by NABARD offices at every level across the country. Interest rate revisions by the Asset–Liability Committee The Asset–Liability Committee (ALCO), which meets at least once every month, is responsible for strategic management of interest rate and liquidity risks, taking into account the interest rate forecasts and expected spreads. It takes care of the pricing of refinance/ direct finance loans and assesses its impact on the net interest income. ALCO decides on the desired maturity profile and takes appropriate decisions on the mix of incremental assets and liabilities. It also monitors market risk and ensures adherence to various risk limits set by the Board. Risk reassessment of refinance proposals To strengthen risk assessment procedures, risk reassessment of the refinance proposals of commercial banks, non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), NBFC-microfinance institutions, small finance banks, state cooperative banks, and other client agencies is undertaken before it is taken up for sanction by the business departments. During FY2023, risk reassessment has been undertaken for 46 refinance proposals amounting to ₹93,838 crore. | 
 | Risk control and self-assessment The risk control and self-assessment (RCSA) exercise as one of the tools of the operational risk management framework has been undertaken to ascertain inherent risks, identify specific controls, perform assessment and rating of the controls, and generate health index for the RCSA units (Head Office departments, regional offices, and training establishments). Note: ERMS = Enterprise Risk Management System. |

Particulars of the Key Audit Matter | Audit processes in the matter
Multiple IT Systems: The Bank is dependent on technology considering significant number of transactions that are processed daily across multiple and discrete Information Technology (‘IT’) systems. The audit approach relies extensively on several reports generated by interface of these IT systems and inbuilt automated controls therein. The major IT systems concerning the financial reporting process include: • CLMAS – transactions processing, workflows and financial reporting system • TALMS – Treasury Operations • Empower HRMS – HR and payroll • FAMS – Property, Plant and Equipment and processing of expenses • Interface/interplay of one or more of above systems in building up or generating reports IT general and application controls are critical to ensure that changes to applications and underlying data are made in an appropriate manner. Adequate controls contribute to mitigating the risk of potential fraud or errors as a result of changes to the applications and data. Management of the Bank continuously endeavors several remediation activities and is in the process of bettering the implementation thereof aiming at minimization of the risks over IT applications in the financial reporting process. These includes implementation of preventive and detective controls across critical applications and infrastructure. Due to the pervasive nature, in our preliminary risk assessment, we planned our audit by assessing the risk of a material misstatement arising from the technology as significant for the audit, hence the Key Audit Matter. | We performed a range of audit procedures, which included: Review of the report of IS Audit carried out for half year ending June, 2021 and December 2021 by an independent firm of Chartered Accountants pertaining to IT systems, general controls including access rights over applications, operating systems and databases relied upon for financial reporting. Our audit tests were designed to cover the following: • understanding the Bank’s IT control environment and key changes in the course of our audit that were considered relevant to the audit; • selectively recomputing interest calculations and maturity dates; • Selectively re-evaluating masters updation, interface with resultant reports; • Selective testing of the interface of CLMAS with other IT systems like TALMS, Empower and several workflows; • Having regard to the incidences of incorrect system entries getting posted in the accounting system, detailed inquiries were made into ‘root cause analysis’ and about lack of adequate checks and balances around such entries, to obtain suitable explanations and representations. • Testing of the system generated reports and accounting entries manually for core financial reporting matters (i.e. verification around the computer system), so as to rectify the incorrect entries noticed during the audit. • To avoid the scope of incorrect system entries, to have more useful system generated reports and to include more features/ fields into the system, the development of CLMAS 2.0 is under process.

Particulars of the Key Audit Matter in respect of the Holding Bank | Audit processes in the matter
Multiple IT Systems: The Holding Bank is dependent on technology considering significant number of transactions that are processed daily across multiple and discrete Information Technology (‘IT’) systems. The audit approach relies extensively on several reports generated by interface of these IT systems and inbuilt automated controls therein. The major IT systems concerning the financial reporting process include: • CLMAS – transactions processing, workflows and financial reporting system • TALMS – Treasury Operations • Empower HRMS – HR and payroll • FAMS – Property, Plant and Equipment and processing of expenses • Interface/interplay of one or more of above systems in building up or generating reports IT general and application controls are critical to ensure that changes to applications and underlying data are made in an appropriate manner. Adequate controls contribute to mitigating the risk of potential fraud or errors as a result of changes to the applications and data. Management of the Holding Bank continuously endeavors several remediation activities and is in the process of bettering the implementation thereof aiming at minimization of the risks over IT applications in the financial reporting process. These includes implementation of preventive and detective controls across critical applications and infrastructure. Due to the pervasive nature, in our preliminary risk assessment, we planned our audit by assessing the risk of a material misstatement arising from the technology as significant for the audit, hence the Key Audit Matter. | We performed a range of audit procedures in course of the audit of Standalone Financial Statements of the Holding Bank, which included: Review of the report of IS Audit carried out for half year ending June, 2021 and December 2021 by an independent firm of Chartered Accountants pertaining to IT systems general controls including access rights over applications, operating systems and databases relied upon for financial reporting. Our audit tests were designed to cover the following: • understanding the Bank’s IT control environment and key changes in the course of our audit that were considered relevant to the audit; • selectively recomputing interest calculations and maturity dates; • Selectively re-evaluating masters updation, interface with resultant reports; • Selective testing of the interface of CLMAS with other IT systems like TALMS, Empower and several workflows; • Having regard to the incidences of incorrect system entries getting posted in the accounting system, detailed inquiries were made into ‘root cause analysis’ and about lack of adequate checks and balances around such entries, to obtain suitable explanations and representations. • Testing of the system generated reports and accounting entries manually for core financial reporting matters (i.e. verification around the computer system), so as to rectify the incorrect entries noticed during the audit. • To avoid the scope of incorrect system entries, have more useful system generated reports and to include more features/ fields into the system, the development of CLMAS 2.0 is under process.
